title: "Number of ratings, rater differences, and score reliability in creativity ratings of football actions: A judge response theory analysis"

abstract: |
  The consensual assessment technique (CAT) is the standard procedure for rating creative products and is also used for actions in sport. However, little is known about how reliable such scores are when each action receives only some ratings, or how much raters differ in judging creativity in sport. In this exploratory study, 19 student raters gave 7,820 ratings of 3,668 football actions on a 7-point creativity scale. We fitted a graded response model (GRM) and a judge response theory ladder from the rating-scale many-facet Rasch model to the generalized partial credit model. The empirical reliability of the obtained scores was .672, against .960 for a hypothetical full panel; mean product-level reliability was .520 for actions with one rating and .698 with two. Raters differed in category use (raw share of lowest-category ratings: .579 to .016), threshold location and discrimination; parameters of raters with few ratings were imprecise. Likelihood-ratio tests rejected a shared rating-scale structure and equal discrimination (both *p* < .001), although BIC favoured equal discrimination. Among actions with one and two ratings, raw mean ratings and GRM scores agreed with Kendall's $\tau_b$ = .832 and .815. For similar rater pools, studies should report the reliability of the scores used, plan ratings per action accordingly and, because some rater parameters were imprecise, consider linking raters through a common calibration set. Because raters differed and raw means ordered actions partly differently, studies should consider model-based scoring that adjusts for rater differences and report how far it departs from raw means.

# Introduction

Creativity is widely regarded as a core competence. Employers rank creative thinking among the core skills of the workforce [@wef2025], the Programme for International Student Assessment assessed creative thinking in its 2022 cycle [@oecd2024], and in sport, creativity is considered a key quality to be developed and evaluated in players [@safardilha2019; @santos2016]. [\[FILL IN: verify these framing claims and those attributed to memmert2011, batey2012 and barbot2019b against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Creativity research distinguishes four facets: the creative person, the creative process, the creative product and the press, that is, the environment in which creativity occurs [@batey2012]. Each facet requires its own measurement approach [@barbot2019; @barbot2019b]. The present paper is concerned with the product facet, namely actions performed in football matches, as judged by others.

The consensual assessment technique (CAT) is the established method for evaluating creative products [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011; @kaufman2024]. In the CAT and judge response theory literature, raters are called judges; we use "raters" throughout. In the CAT, raters who are familiar with the domain rate products independently and relative to one another [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. Independent raters usually reach coefficient alphas above .70 [@baer2004; @kaufman2008a; @hennessey2011] [\[FILL IN: verify the ".70" claim against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}, but considerably lower agreement has also been reported and attributed to differences between raters in procedure, scale use and beliefs about creativity [@long2015; @cseh2019].

The reliability of CAT scores rests on the number of raters. As @amabile1982 noted, the Spearman–Brown reliability of an aggregated rating depends on the mean inter-rater correlation and on the number of raters, so that a larger panel compensates for lower agreement between individual raters. Conversely, a high alpha from a large panel can mask low agreement among individual raters [@kaufman2008a]. A rule of thumb of five to ten raters is often cited [@kaufman2008], but @cseh2019 argue that the number of raters needed for adequate reliability has to be established for each domain. A further distinction matters when many products are rated. A panel coefficient describes the mean over all raters of a panel; when each product receives only some of the possible ratings, what matters for the use of a score is the precision of that product's score, given the ratings it actually received [@primi2019; @forthmann2025]. [\[FILL IN: verify kaufman2008 ("five to ten"), kaufman2008a ("a high alpha can mask low agreement"), the cseh2019 paraphrase, and that primi2019 and forthmann2025 support the point on product-level precision (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Raters also differ systematically, in severity, in their use of the rating scale and in their beliefs about creativity [@long2015], and their tendencies can drift over time [@barth2021]. Research on rater-mediated assessment describes such differences as rater effects, including severity, central tendency, restriction of range and halo [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. In judged sports, the accuracy and bias of judges have been monitored with Rasch-family or other statistical models, although for performance quality rather than creativity [@looney2004; @anderlucci2021; @heiniger2021]. [\[FILL IN: verify this characterisation of looney2004, anderlucci2021 and heiniger2021 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

How rater differences are handled depends on the scoring model. Unweighted mean ratings treat raters as interchangeable. Whenever different raters rate different products, mean scores are therefore confounded with the severity of the raters who happened to rate each product [@primi2019]. Coefficient alpha requires only essential $\tau$-equivalence, which allows raters to differ in their intercepts, that is, in severity [@myszkowski2019]; a raw mean in an incomplete design, however, does not adjust for these intercepts. The many-facet Rasch model (MFRM) adds rater severity as a facet and thereby adjusts for it [@linacre1989; @eckes2015; @primi2019].

Severity is not the only way in which raters differ. Item response theory (IRT) models the probability of each response as a function of a latent attribute and of item parameters [@lord1980; @embretson2013; @ayala2022]. Rasch models constrain all items to discriminate equally [@rasch1960; @bond2020], and their polytomous extensions, the rating scale model [RSM, @andrich1978] and the partial credit model [PCM, @masters1982], differ in whether all items share one category structure. Accordingly, the rating-scale form of the MFRM assumes that all raters share one category structure, whereas a partial-credit MFRM gives each rater their own thresholds [@eckes2015]. [\[FILL IN: verify eckes2015 as the source for the partial-credit (rater-related scale structure) MFRM (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Every Rasch-family model, including the partial-credit form, assumes equal discrimination, so that differences in discrimination have no parameter and surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]. Judge response theory (JRT) treats raters as items with their own discrimination and thresholds, for instance in the generalized partial credit model [GPCM, @muraki1992] or the graded response model [GRM, @samejima1969], and yields scores with product-specific standard errors as well as an explicit description of rater behaviour [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. JRT has been applied in recent creativity research [@barbot2023; @pellegrino2025], and @pellegrino2025 retained a GRM. [\[FILL IN: verify that pellegrino2025 retained a GRM (FI-17)\]]{.mark} The RSM, PCM and GPCM are nested adjacent-category models whose constraints can be tested by likelihood-ratio tests. The GRM is a cumulative model, which arguably matches a scale on which raters express an increasing amount of creativity [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-8\]]{.mark}; it can be compared with the adjacent-category models by information criteria.

Creativity research in sport has focused mainly on the creative process, for example on divergent thinking [@memmert2011]. Ratings of creative actions exist as well. @kempe2018 obtained ratings of actions in competition from trained experts, using a scale that originated in expert ratings of tactical creativity [@memmert2007], and further studies have rated football actions [@zahno2023; @joode2023]. These studies average the ratings and report intraclass correlations or agreement [\[FILL IN: verify this characterisation of kempe2018, zahno2023 and joode2023 against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}; a Rasch analysis exists only for a coach-completed questionnaire that rates players rather than actions [@shin2025]. However, three gaps remain. First, little is known about how the reliability of creativity scores of sport actions depends on the number of ratings each action receives, although the number of raters needed for adequate reliability has to be established for each domain [@cseh2019]. Second, there is no evidence on how raters differ when they judge the creativity of sport actions. Third, to our knowledge, rater differences have not been modelled with IRT or JRT for creativity ratings in sport. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-2: the literature search was not systematic\]]{.mark}

## The present study

The present study analysed CAT-style creativity ratings of football actions given by multiple raters. It was exploratory and had three aims: to describe the reliability of the creativity scores, overall and by the number of ratings per action; to describe how raters differ; and to describe how much the scores depend on whether rater differences are modelled. No confirmatory hypotheses were formulated. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-20: exploratory framing and RQ wording\]]{.mark}

- **RQ1.** How reliable are the creativity scores obtained in this study, and how does the reliability of an action's score vary with the number of ratings it received? How does the reliability of the obtained scores compare with that of a hypothetical full panel and with conventional agreement and consistency indices?
- **RQ2.** How do raters differ in threshold location, scale use, discrimination and information, and how precisely are these differences estimated?
- **RQ3.** (a) Are the constraints of a shared category structure (rating-scale MFRM) and of equal discrimination (all Rasch-family models, including the partial-credit MFRM) tenable for these ratings? (b) How far do scores and rankings change when rater differences are ignored (raw mean ratings) or constrained (rating-scale MFRM, partial-credit MFRM, GPCM)?

To answer these questions, we fitted a ladder of JRT models and a GRM by marginal maximum likelihood, estimated the reliability of the obtained scores overall and by number of ratings, described the rater parameters with their uncertainty, and compared GRM scores with raw mean ratings. Rater expertise and the design of the rating scale are not analysed.

# Method

## Overview

This was a CAT-style rating study in which raters independently rated the creativity of football actions in a randomised order [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. The ratings were collected as part of a larger project. [\[FILL IN: context and purpose of the larger project (FI-1, FI-2)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: ethics approval (committee, reference number) and informed-consent procedure (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The analyses were exploratory. [\[FILL IN: preregistration status (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

## Raters

Raters were Bachelor's and Master's students who rated as part of their thesis projects. [\[FILL IN: confirm; recruitment and number of raters at the start (FI-1)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description - football playing or coaching experience, any instruction or practice before rating, number of sessions per rater, demographics and compensation, or a statement that these were not recorded (FI-21)\]]{.mark} The final data comprised 19 raters, pseudonymised as R01 to R19, who gave between 50 and 1,174 ratings each (column "Ratings by rater" in the rater tables, e.g., @tbl-grm-rater-parameters); the three excluded raters are R20 to R22.

## Products and stimulus material

Each rated product was a single football action; we use "product" for the analyses and "action" when referring to the football content. Actions were shown as video clips from recorded football matches and were identified with event data. [\[FILL IN: competitions and matches, action-selection rule, clip length, video source and number of matches (FI-2)\]]{.mark}

## Rating procedure

[\[FILL IN: rating software (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters were shown an instruction that defined creativity as the combination of originality and functionality of an action in its game context [@runco2012]. [\[FILL IN: verbatim instruction and creativity definition, original language and English translation (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Showing a definition departs to a minor degree from the CAT rule that raters receive no criteria [@hennessey2011] and resembles the procedure of trained-rater studies in sport [@kempe2018; @memmert2007]. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-19\]]{.mark} Creativity was rated on a unipolar 7-point scale with verbal anchors at 1, 4 and 7. [\[FILL IN: verify the anchors and give their wording (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters could also mark a clip as "action not recognised". [\[FILL IN: exact wording of this option (FI-3)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: randomisation procedure, session length and breaks, and the data-collection period (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters also rated technical correctness and aesthetic appeal, which are not analysed here. [\[FILL IN: wording and scales of these dimensions (FI-3)\]]{.mark}

## Rating design

[\[FILL IN: allocation of products to raters - planned overlap, any common or benchmark set, randomisation, thesis-specific subsets or rater dropout; how products came to have 1, 2 or 3+ ratings; whether products with different numbers of ratings were rated by different raters or differ systematically (match, action type) (FI-4)\]]{.mark} Not every rater rated every product. The design was incomplete but connected: all raters and products formed a single connected component, so that all rater parameters and product scores lie on one scale [@eckes2015]. Marginal maximum likelihood estimation assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the design. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-18: if a planned benchmark set rated by all raters was not realised as a fully crossed block, state this here\]]{.mark}

## Data preparation and final data

The raw export contained 9,148 rows. The 1,290 ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; such ratings result from video cutting and imperfect material, where close-ups or other TV artefacts render the action non-visible. [\[FILL IN: rate of "action not recognised" ratings by rater and, if available, by product (FI-22)\]]{.mark} One out-of-range value (0.0, given by R04) was removed. Twelve rater–product pairs had been entered more than once, one of them with conflicting values; the last entry was kept, which removed 13 rows. This left 7,844 ratings by 22 raters.

Raters with fewer than 15 ratings were excluded because their up to seven rater-specific parameters cannot be estimated reliably: R20 (13 ratings), R21 (9) and R22 (2), together 24 ratings (@tbl-excluded-raters). [\[FILL IN: source or rationale for the exclusion criterion of 15 ratings (FI-23)\]]{.mark} One product rated only by these raters was dropped. Excluding them changed the product scores only slightly [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-26\]]{.mark}, with a largest change in a product score of 0.16246 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion).

The final data are described in @tbl-design-summary: 7,820 ratings of 3,668 products by 19 raters, given on the scale 1–7 and coded 0–6 internally. Products received a mean of 2.132 ratings (median 2, range 1–10, harmonic mean 1.726; @fig-overview-degree-distributions). The product-by-rater matrix had a fill of .112 and formed one connected component; 17 of the 171 rater pairs had no product in common, and the median overlap of rater pairs was 13 products. Five raters left categories at the top of the scale unused: category 7 was never used by R01, R03, R06 and R18, and categories 6 and 7 were never used by R17 (@tbl-category-usage). No rater had an unused category inside their observed range. Because thresholds are estimated only between categories a rater used, these raters have fewer thresholds.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-design-summary >}}

## Measurement models

All models share the JRT frame [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]: raters take the role of items, products the role of persons, and product creativity is a single latent dimension $\theta$ with a standard normal distribution. A rater's threshold $b_k$ is the $\theta$ at which a rating above category $k$ becomes more likely than a rating of $k$ or below. The discrimination $a$ expresses how sharply a rater's ratings separate products of different creativity. In the GRM, thresholds are expressed relative to discrimination, so threshold spacing is partly the same fact as discrimination.

The adjacent-category ladder comprised three nested models. M1, the rating-scale MFRM, was the rating scale model [@andrich1978] with raters as items; it corresponds to a two-facet rating-scale MFRM with products and raters as facets [@linacre1989; @eckes2015; @primi2019], here estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with a normal product distribution in `sirt::rm.facets` [@robitzsch2025]. M1 gives each rater a severity and is the only model in the ladder in which all raters share one category structure. M2, the partial-credit MFRM, was the partial credit model [@masters1982] with raters as items. It gives each rater their own thresholds, corresponds to a partial-credit MFRM [@eckes2015] and, like every Rasch model, assumes equal discrimination. M3, the GPCM [@muraki1992], additionally gives each rater their own discrimination. M2 and M3 were estimated with the R package mirt [@chalmers2012].

The retained scoring model was a GRM with rater-specific discriminations and thresholds [@samejima1969], estimated in mirt; its thresholds are ordered by construction. It was estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm (61 quadrature points, tolerance $10^{-4}$), with standard errors from Oakes' identity [@chalmers2018]. The model converged after 165 iterations with a positive definite information matrix (@tbl-grm-convergence).

## Model comparison

Two likelihood-ratio (LR) tests were computed within the ladder: M1 (rating-scale MFRM) versus M2 (partial-credit MFRM) for a shared versus a rater-specific category structure, and M2 versus M3 (GPCM) for equal versus rater-specific discriminations. For all four models, the log-likelihood, AIC, BIC and the sample-size adjusted BIC (SABIC) were computed, with the difference to the best model on each criterion. The GRM, which is not nested in the ladder, was compared by information criteria only. Three caveats apply. The M1–M2 test compares models estimated in different software (sirt and mirt), so it is approximate. Its degrees of freedom are below the formula value $(J-1)(K-2)$ for $J$ raters and $K$ categories, because a rater who never used an end category has one step parameter fewer in M2 (@tbl-category-usage). Finally, no model without rater effects was fitted, so severity differences were not tested on their own.

## Model adequacy

Infit and outfit mean squares [@wright1982] were computed for each rater under M1 and the GRM. Their expected value is 1, and no misfit cut-offs were applied; values below 1 are expected because each product's score is estimated from the ratings being checked. The S-X² statistic [@orlando2000; @kang2008] requires complete data, so the missing ratings were imputed 20 times from the fitted model and the statistic was averaged. About 90% of the cells were imputed, so the test has little power. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-11\]]{.mark} Local dependence was examined with Yen's Q3 [@yen1984], the correlation of two raters' residuals over the products both rated. Q3 was computed for rater pairs with at least 3 jointly rated products and residual variance in both raters (137 of 171 pairs). Because Q3 is negatively biased when few raters rate each product [@christensen2017], pairs were compared by their deviation from the mean Q3 over all computable pairs. A pair was flagged when it had at least 30 jointly rated products and deviated from this mean by more than 0.2. This criterion has no reference distribution. The global statistic C2 [@cai2014] could not be computed, because it needs the joint distribution of every rater pair and 17 of 171 pairs share no products.

## Scores and reliability

Product scores were expected a posteriori (EAP) estimates $\hat\theta$ with the posterior standard deviation (PSD) as their standard error. The primary index was the empirical marginal reliability of the scores actually obtained, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) / [\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \overline{\mathrm{PSD}^2}]$. For comparison, the model-based marginal reliability [@green1984], which refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters, was computed with mirt and checked on a $\theta$ grid. Ninety-five percent intervals for both came from 200 accepted draws of the parameters from their asymptotic normal distribution (estimates and Oakes covariance matrix); for the empirical reliability, products were also resampled. A draw that did not define a valid GRM (some $a \leq 0$ or thresholds out of order) was rejected and replaced; 87 draws were rejected. The intervals are therefore conditional on valid parameter sets and approximate, especially for raters with few ratings.

At the product level, rel~post~ $= 1 - \mathrm{PSD}^2$ was computed. Because it is defined relative to the unit prior variance of $\theta$, it partly reflects the prior when a product has one or two ratings. As a check, rel~info~ $= I/(I+1)$ was computed from the information $I$ of the product's own raters at $\hat\theta$. Both were summarised by the number of ratings each product received (column "Ratings per product" in @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n).

Conventional reliability indices assume a complete design or must be adapted to an incomplete one [@hove2024], so we report them only as reference values for common practice. Cronbach's alpha [@cronbach1951] was computed from pairwise covariances over all usable raters and on the largest fully crossed block of raters and products [\[FILL IN: why five raters (R19, R14, R02, R16, R12) were not usable for the pairwise alpha; optionally, which three raters form the crossed block (FI-9)\]]{.mark}, and Krippendorff's ordinal alpha [@hayes2007] measured the agreement of single ratings. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals came from bootstrapping products (1,000 replications). For the pairwise alpha, 639 of the 1,000 replications could be computed; in the other 361, some rater pair lost all shared products. The interval rests on the computable replications and is approximate and possibly biased. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-11\]]{.mark}

As a side note, the reliability expected for 1 to 10 ratings per product was projected from the fitted GRM, with raters drawn at random from this panel (see the supplement, @tbl-grm-reliability-projection).

## Rater parameters, information and response styles

The GRM discrimination $a$ and thresholds $b_k$ of each rater were reported with their standard errors. Rater information integrated over the standard normal distribution of $\theta$ is called the rater's average information; each rater's share of the full-panel information was computed overall and at selected values of $\theta$. Ninety-five percent intervals came from the same parameter draws as above. Descriptive response styles on the raw 1–7 scale (@tbl-overview-rater-response-styles) comprised each rater's mean, median, standard deviation, interquartile range, number of categories used, entropy (natural logarithm), and the shares of ratings in the lowest category (1; floor), the highest category (7; ceiling), the extreme categories (1, 7) and the middle categories (3–5; central); they are not adjusted for which products each rater saw.

## Score agreement and sensitivity

Each product's raw mean rating, the common-practice score that treats raters as interchangeable, was compared with its GRM score separately for products with one, two, and three or more ratings. Because the raw mean takes few distinct values (with one rating, only seven), agreement was described by Kendall's $\tau_b$, by the share of product pairs with different raw means that the GRM score orders the other way round (pairs in reversed order), and by the mean and maximum range of GRM scores among products with the same raw mean. To describe the dependence on the choice among the four models, the EAP scores of all models were correlated (Pearson and Spearman); relative to the GRM, the absolute shift in percentile rank (0–1 scale) and the share of products changing quintile were computed. M1 was also re-estimated with the default integration grid of sirt as a check. Finally, the GRM was refitted with all 22 raters.

## Software and availability

All models were estimated in R with mirt [@chalmers2012] and sirt [@robitzsch2025]; psych and a Krippendorff package were used for the conventional indices, and Python for display. [\[FILL IN: versions of R, mirt, sirt, psych and the Krippendorff package (FI-6)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: data and code availability statement; only pseudonymised rater IDs are shared (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

# Results

The results follow the three aims: the reliability of the scores, the differences between raters, and the dependence of the scores on modelling rater differences. All analyses used the final data in @tbl-design-summary. We first report the scoring model.

## Scoring model

As shown in @tbl-model-fit, the GRM had the lowest AIC, BIC and SABIC of the four models. The GRM and M3 (GPCM) have the same number of parameters (127), so their comparison reduces to the log-likelihood (−11,733.227 vs. −11,756.510), and the GRM is lower by 46.566 on AIC, BIC and SABIC alike. No rater's S-X² was significant (*p* from .294 to .671; @tbl-grm-rater-fit). Infit ranged from 0.334 (R19) to 0.971 (R18) and outfit from 0.322 (R19) to 0.961 (R18), all below 1. The mean Q3 over the 137 computable pairs was −.238, and 20 pairs were flagged; of the 10 shown in @tbl-grm-q3-flagged, nine deviated negatively and one (R10–R11) positively. C2 could not be computed (see Model adequacy).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-model-fit >}}

## Reliability of the creativity scores and number of ratings

@tbl-reliability-overview sets the reliability of the obtained scores against the other indices and states what each refers to. The empirical marginal reliability of the obtained scores was .672 [.649, .687]. The model-based marginal reliability for a hypothetical product rated by all raters was .960 [.953, .968], with a grid check of .960 (@tbl-grm-reliability-ci; @fig-grm-panel-information). Cronbach's alpha from pairwise covariances was .928 [.891, .943] (14 raters, 1,900 products); its interval is approximate, because it rests on the 639 of 1,000 bootstrap replications that could be computed (@tbl-naive-indices). On the fully crossed block, Cronbach's alpha was .658 [.526, .756] (3 raters, 139 products). Krippendorff's ordinal alpha, which refers to the agreement of single ratings, was .392 [.362, .417] (19 raters, 2,771 products).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-reliability-overview >}}

@tbl-grm-reliability-by-n summarises product-level reliability by the number of ratings each product received. Mean rel~post~ was .520 for the 897 products with one rating, .698 for the 2,080 products with two and .757 for the 357 products with three, and it was higher with each further rating in the table, up to .919 for the three products with ten ratings. Mean PSD fell from 0.686 to 0.285. The rows for nine and ten ratings rest on three products each, and no mean reached the full-panel value of .960. Products with the same number of ratings differed in rel~post~ (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-n). These values are observed: products did not receive their number of ratings through a design manipulation (see Rating design). [\[FILL IN: how products came to have their number of ratings (FI-4)\]]{.mark}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-reliability-by-n >}}

Across all products, rel~post~ had a median of .698 and an interquartile range of .173 (first and third quartiles .596 and .769), with values from .057 to .929 (@tbl-grm-reliability-summary; @fig-grm-rel-post-histogram); its relation to $\hat\theta$ is shown in @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta. rel~post~ and rel~info~ correlated at *r* = .935, and 320 products differed by more than .1 (@fig-grm-rel-consistency).

## Rater differences

@fig-overview-rater-response-styles describes the raters on the raw scale; the values are given in @tbl-overview-rater-response-styles. Rater means ranged from 1.760 (R06) to 3.836 (R18) and standard deviations from 1.022 (R01) to 1.953 (R19). The share of ratings in the lowest category (1) ranged from .579 (R06) to .016 (R13). The share in the highest category (7) was highest for R19 (.080), and five raters (R01, R03, R06, R17 and R18) gave no ratings of 7. The share in the middle categories (3–5) was highest for R13 (.799), followed by R18 (.764) and R12 (.735), and lowest for R06 (.192). Across all ratings, category 1 received 2,029 ratings and category 2 received 2,113, whereas category 7 was the rarest, with 109 (@fig-overview-rating-distribution). These response-style values are descriptive and have no per-rater uncertainty.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/01_data_overview.ipynb#fig-overview-rater-response-styles >}}

@tbl-grm-rater-parameters gives the GRM parameters with their standard errors; the category response functions are shown in @fig-grm-category-response-functions. Over all 19 raters, first thresholds $b_1$ ranged from −6.56 (R18, 55 ratings, *SE* 3.05) to 0.29 (R06, *SE* 0.06); the next lowest was −3.38 (R13, *SE* 0.49), and R06 was the only rater with a positive $b_1$. Threshold spacing also differed, for example from −0.71 ($b_1$) to 2.03 ($b_6$) for R02 and from −3.38 to 4.43 for R13; in the GRM, spacing is partly the same fact as discrimination. R17 had four thresholds, R01, R03, R06 and R18 had five, and all other raters had six.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-rater-parameters >}}

Discrimination ranged from 0.63 (R18, 55 ratings, *SE* 0.26) to 3.71 (R19, 50 ratings, *SE* 2.22). The next highest value was 3.70 (R16, 52 ratings, *SE* 1.36) and the next lowest 0.86 (R09, 400 ratings, *SE* 0.15). Raters with many ratings had, for example, 1.96 (R01, *SE* 0.16), 2.50 (R02, *SE* 0.33) and 2.81 (R06, *SE* 0.42).

Average information and information shares are given with 95% intervals, based on the same 200 accepted parameter draws, in @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci. Average information ranged from 0.12 [0.01, 0.35] (R18) to 3.54 [0.41, 11.02] (R19), with R16 at 3.30 [0.73, 6.49]; shares ranged from .005 [.000, .013] (R18) to .135 [.017, .331] (R19). Raters with many ratings had, for example, 0.24 [0.11, 0.42] (R09), 0.98 [0.72, 1.22] (R01) and 1.70 [0.90, 2.56] (R02).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-rater-information-ci >}}

Raters provided information in different regions of the latent scale (@fig-grm-rater-information; @tbl-grm-information-summary). The location of maximum information was highest for R01 (2.700) and R06 (2.400), neither of whom used category 7, and lowest for R13 (−0.550). Shares varied with $\theta$ (@fig-grm-information-shares): R06 contributed .001 at $\theta = -2$ and .083 at $\theta = +2$, whereas R12 contributed .221 at $\theta = -2$.

## Dependence of the scores on modelling rater differences

The LR test of M1 (rating-scale MFRM) against M2 (partial-credit MFRM), which concerns the shared category structure of M1, gave $\chi^2(84) = 737.457$, *p* < .001 (@tbl-lr-tests). The test of M2 against M3 (GPCM), which concerns equal discrimination, gave $\chi^2(18) = 121.958$, *p* < .001. AIC favoured M3 over M2 (23,767.020 vs. 23,852.978), whereas BIC ranked M2 (24,529.585) below M3 (24,555.360). Rater-specific discriminations were thus supported by the LR test and AIC, but not by BIC.

Within the ladder, M3 discriminations ranged from 0.283 (R09, *SE* 0.055) to 2.606 (R16, *SE* 1.419) (@tbl-discrimination-m3). Nine raters had unordered step parameters under M2 and nine under M3 (@tbl-threshold-order). Under M1, only R17 (infit 1.328, outfit 1.190) and R18 (1.009, 1.071) had values at or above 1, and R12 had the lowest (0.238, 0.255; @tbl-rater-fit-m1).

@tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm and @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta compare each product's raw mean rating with its GRM score within groups of products with the same number of ratings. For the 897 products with one rating, Kendall's $\tau_b$ was .832, and .042 of the pairs with different raw means were in reversed order. Products with the same single rating received GRM scores that spanned on average 1.283 and at most 1.436; in the one-rating panel of @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta, this appears as vertical spread at each rating (points are jittered horizontally). For the 2,080 products with two ratings, $\tau_b$ was .815, .067 of the pairs were in reversed order, and the range of GRM scores at equal raw mean was 1.537 on average and 2.196 at most. For the 691 products with three or more ratings, the values were .842, .070, 0.619 and 1.396.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm >}}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-raw-mean-vs-theta >}}

@tbl-score-agreement compares the scores of the constrained models with the GRM scores. Relative to the GRM, M1 (rating-scale MFRM) scores correlated at .975 (Pearson) and .978 (Spearman), and .202 of products changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .042. For M2 (partial-credit MFRM), the correlations were .985 and .983, and .150 of products changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .033; for M3 (GPCM), they were .996 and .996, and .075 changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .017. Among the ladder models, Pearson correlations ranged from .980 to .993 and Spearman correlations from .983 to .996 (@tbl-theta-correlations); M1 re-estimated with the default integration grid correlated at 1.000 with M1.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-score-agreement >}}

No confidence intervals are available for these agreement statistics. The contrast between M1 and the GRM combines the rater constraints with a change of link function. All comparisons show that the scores differ, not which score is more accurate.

## Sensitivity to the rater exclusion

Refitting the GRM with all 22 raters (7,844 ratings, 3,669 products) changed the empirical marginal reliability from .67199 to .67186 and the model-based marginal reliability from .95986 to .96186 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion). Over the 3,668 common products, the scores of the two fits correlated at .99997 (Pearson); the mean absolute difference was 0.00171, the maximum 0.16246, and .00491 of products changed quintile. Over the 19 common raters, discriminations correlated at .99880, with a maximum absolute difference of 0.19820.

# Discussion

This study described the reliability of creativity scores for football actions, the differences between raters, and the dependence of the scores on whether rater differences are modelled. The reliability of the obtained scores was well below that of a hypothetical full panel, and product-level reliability was lower for products with fewer ratings. Raters differed in category use, threshold location, discrimination and information, with imprecise estimates for raters with few ratings. The shared category structure of M1 (rating-scale MFRM) was rejected; equal discrimination, which all Rasch-family models assume, was rejected by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC. Within each number of ratings, raw means and GRM scores ordered a non-trivial share of products differently ($\tau_b$ from .815 to .842). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-22\]]{.mark} These results rest on the GRM, which had the lowest values on all information criteria.

## Reliability and the number of ratings per action

The conventional figures describe the mean over a large or complete panel: the full-panel reliability was .960 and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha .928. The scores actually obtained had an empirical reliability of .672 [.649, .687], and this is the figure that matters when the scores are used. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-3\]]{.mark} The difference follows the Spearman–Brown logic described by @amabile1982: the panel coefficients refer to more ratings per product than the products received. The contrast between Krippendorff's alpha for single ratings (.392) and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha (.928) illustrates the point of @kaufman2008a that a high alpha can hide low agreement between individual raters. The alpha of the fully crossed block (.658, three raters) lay close to the empirical reliability, although the two indices refer to different quantities. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-13\]]{.mark}

Actions with one rating had a mean product-level reliability of .520, and actions with two ratings .698. Where individual action scores are used, for example to select creative actions, one or two ratings per action gave limited precision in these data. Precision also differed among products with the same number of ratings and with their location on $\theta$ (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-n; @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta), and for one or two ratings, rel~post~ partly reflects the prior. @cseh2019 argue that the number of raters needed for adequate reliability has to be established for each domain; these values describe this football rating task and this rater pool. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-4, ATC-5; see ATC-2 on novelty\]]{.mark} As a side note, a simple projection from the fitted GRM, with raters drawn at random from this panel (each rater equally likely) and the parameters treated as known, gives an empirical reliability of .508 for one rating, .688 for two and .925 for ten ratings per product (@tbl-grm-reliability-projection and @fig-grm-reliability-projection in the supplement), which gauges the value of adding ratings in this rater pool. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-5\]]{.mark}

## Raters differ

The raters spanned a wide range of category use, threshold location and discrimination. For raters with many ratings, the differences clearly exceeded the standard errors, for example between R09 ($a$ = 0.86, *SE* 0.15) and R06 (2.81, *SE* 0.42). Because threshold spacing in the GRM is partly the same fact as discrimination, the raw response styles (@tbl-overview-rater-response-styles) carry the model-independent evidence on scale use, although they are not adjusted for which products each rater saw. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-6\]]{.mark} These differences are in line with reports of differing scale use and beliefs among CAT raters [@long2015] and with the rater effects described in rater-mediated assessment [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. The contrast between raters who concentrated their ratings in the middle categories (e.g., R13) and raters who used the lowest category heavily (e.g., R06) corresponds to the central versus extreme responding discussed by @myszkowski2021; @primi2019 left such rater-by-scale interactions to future research. [\[FILL IN: verify the attributions to myszkowski2021 and primi2019 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

The most extreme estimates came from R18, R19 and R16, raters with about 50 ratings who also had the largest standard errors (R18 for its thresholds, R19 and R16 for their discriminations); R19 and R16 also had the widest information intervals. The information shares are therefore not a ranking of rater quality. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-12\]]{.mark} This agrees with work showing that rater estimates in incomplete rating networks depend on the linking set [@wind2018; @wind2019] and that GRM parameter recovery requires adequate numbers of responses [@reise1990]; which rater characteristics predict discernment is a separate question [@ceh2022]. [\[FILL IN: verify the attributions to wind2018, wind2019 and reise1990 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

## Why rater differences matter for scoring

Unweighted means treat raters as interchangeable, and when different raters rate different actions, the means are confounded with rater severity [@primi2019]. In these data, products with the same single rating received GRM scores that spanned on average 1.283 and at most 1.436 (@fig-raw-mean-vs-theta). With one rating, a product's GRM score depends only on that rating and on the parameters of the rater who gave it, so this spread reflects differences between the raters as modelled, in both severity and discrimination; with two or more ratings, it also reflects the different combinations of ratings behind the same mean. As a range, it is set by the most extreme raters for each rating, some of whose parameters are imprecise (R18, R19). Severity on its own was not tested, because no model without rater effects was fitted. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-7, ATC-21\]]{.mark}

The LR test rejected a shared category structure, but this result concerns M1 (rating-scale MFRM); M2 (partial-credit MFRM) already allows each rater their own category structure [@eckes2015]. The Rasch and MFRM family as a whole is questioned only by the discrimination result, and there the criteria disagreed: rater-specific discriminations were supported by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC. Part of the spread in discrimination may also be estimation noise for raters with few ratings. These tests bear on the Rasch and MFRM constraints, not directly on raw-mean averaging. The M1 fit values are consistent with the account that, in Rasch-family models, differences in discrimination surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]: R17, with values above 1 under M1, had a comparatively low GRM discrimination (1.45), whereas R12, with the lowest values under M1, had a high one (2.90). Neither the unordered steps in M2 and M3 nor the ordered GRM thresholds count as evidence for either model family, because unordered steps indicate only that some category is never the most likely response [@andrich1978; @bond2020]. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-7, ATC-9\]]{.mark} A cumulative link is plausible for a unipolar creativity scale, and @pellegrino2025 also retained a GRM for creativity ratings. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-8\]]{.mark}

Rater differences also bear on the ordering of the scores. Within the same number of ratings, raw means and GRM scores agreed with $\tau_b$ = .832 for one rating and .815 for two, and .042 and .067 of the product pairs were in reversed order. With two ratings, the GRM score also depends on the pattern of the two ratings, not only on their mean, so some of the .067 reversals would occur even among identical raters; the one-rating value (.042) is the one that reflects rater differences alone, as modelled. Wherever actions are selected or ranked, for example to compile the most creative actions for training material, such reversals matter. These results agree with @primi2019 and @myszkowski2019 on the limits of averaging. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-22\]]{.mark}

The choice among the models also shifted rankings: although all correlations with the GRM were .975 or higher, .202 of products changed quintile under M1 (rating-scale MFRM), with a mean percentile shift of .042, and .075 under M3 (GPCM), with a mean percentile shift of .017. A quintile change can also be a small move across a quintile boundary, so the two measures are best read together. Because the M1–GRM contrast combines the rater constraints with a change of link function, the two sources cannot be separated here. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-10\]]{.mark}

Neither comparison shows that the GRM scores are more accurate than raw means or the constrained models. The GRM adjusts for the modelled rater differences under its assumptions, but whether it predicts unseen ratings better was not examined. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-15, ATC-22\]]{.mark}

## Practical implications for creativity research in sport

The implications are drawn from one pool of student raters and one 7-point scale and may not transfer unchanged to other rater pools. [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description to qualify this scope (FI-21)\]]{.mark} They are summarised in the box below. Two points need qualification. First, a common calibration set of actions rated by all raters is distinct from rater training; training, unlike a calibration set, conflicts with the CAT rule of independent judgement without imposed criteria [@hennessey2011; @dollinger2005; @storme2014]. A calibration set links the raters more strongly [@wind2019] and stabilises the parameters of raters with few ratings only if these raters rate it and it is large enough. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-14\]]{.mark} Second, about 50 ratings per rater still left the parameters imprecise in these data, so no smaller number can be recommended from them. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-16\]]{.mark}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Design recommendations for creativity ratings in sport"}
1. Report the reliability of the scores actually used (empirical marginal reliability, product standard errors), not only alpha or full-panel values (see @tbl-reliability-overview).
2. Plan the number of ratings per action with the precision of individual scores in mind; in these data, product-level reliability was markedly lower for actions with one or two ratings (see @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n).
3. Where some raters contribute few ratings, let all raters rate a common calibration set of actions, so that raters are more strongly linked and their parameters more precisely estimated (the present design was already connected).
4. Give each rater enough ratings for stable parameters; about 50 ratings per rater still left them imprecise here (see @tbl-grm-rater-parameters and @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci).
5. Raters differed in thresholds and discrimination, and raw means ordered actions partly differently from model-based scores (see @tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm). Consider scoring actions with a model that adjusts for rater differences, under that model's assumptions, and report how far its ordering departs from the raw mean. This study does not show that model-based scores are more accurate.

[\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23 (selection and wording of all items), ATC-3, ATC-5, ATC-14, ATC-15, ATC-16, ATC-22\]]{.mark}
:::

## Limitations and future research

First, the rating design was incomplete, and the analysis assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the allocation of products to raters. [\[FILL IN: allocation procedure (FI-4)\]]{.mark} Ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; if non-recognition depended on the action or the rater, the missingness is not ignorable. [\[FILL IN: non-recognition rate by rater (FI-22)\]]{.mark} The reliabilities by number of ratings are observational.

Second, the fit evidence is limited: S-X² has little power because most cells are imputed, C2 could not be computed, Q3 is negatively biased and its flag criterion has no reference distribution, and infit and outfit below 1 are expected by construction. The absence of detected misfit is therefore not evidence of fit, and the GRM is the best-fitting of the compared models rather than a validated reference. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-11\]]{.mark}

Third, the parameters of raters with few ratings are imprecise, and the parameter-draw intervals are conditional on valid draws. A standard normal latent distribution was assumed, although the ratings concentrated at the low end of the scale. The response styles have no uncertainty, and no confidence intervals exist for the agreement statistics.

Fourth, the raters formed a single pool of students, and whether they meet the CAT's requirement of domain familiarity is not established here. [\[FILL IN: rater-pool characteristics (FI-1, FI-21)\]]{.mark} Expertise was not analysed [@kaufman2009; @kaufman2013; @ceh2022]. Fifth, the exclusion of raters with fewer than 15 ratings was a technical estimation criterion; the largest resulting change in a product score was 0.16246. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-26\]]{.mark}

Sixth, the M1–M2 test of a rating-scale against a partial-credit category structure compares models from different software, with degrees of freedom below the formula value; on equal discrimination, the only constraint common to all Rasch-family models, BIC disagreed with the LR test and AIC; and the M1–GRM contrast mixes rater constraints and link function. Seventh, the models had two facets and one dimension. They contain no facet for time or session, although rater tendencies can drift [@barth2021; @leckie2011; @myford2009] and workload affects agreement [@forthmann2017], and they do not test differential rater functioning [@wind2019a]; models such as the hierarchical rater model [@patz2002] or generalized many-facet models [@uto2020] could address this.

Several analyses were beyond the scope of this descriptive study and are left to future work: a test of rater severity on its own (a model without rater effects against the MFRM), the M1–M2 comparison within one software package, a held-out predictive check of model-based against raw-mean scores, projections that include parameter uncertainty or use selected rater sets, and the number of ratings needed for a target reliability. Future studies should also use a prospective design with a calibration set rated by all raters, include rater covariates such as football expertise, and replicate the analysis in other sports.

# Conclusion

In these data, the reliability of the creativity scores actually obtained for football actions was far below conventional panel figures, and product-level reliability was lower for actions with fewer ratings. Raters differed in category use, threshold location, discrimination and information. The shared category structure of M1 (rating-scale MFRM) was rejected, equal discrimination was rejected by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC, and both raw mean scoring and the constrained models ordered actions partly differently from the GRM. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-1\]]{.mark} For rater pools of this kind, creativity research in sport should report the reliability of the scores it uses, plan the number of ratings per action and, where rater parameters are imprecise, consider linking raters through a common calibration set. Because raters differ and the ordering of actions depends on whether their differences are modelled, researchers should also consider model-based scoring such as judge response theory and report how far it departs from raw means; whether such scores are more accurate remains to be examined. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-5, ATC-14, ATC-15\]]{.mark}

## Projected reliability (side note) {.unnumbered}

Products with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$ were simulated. Each received $k$ ratings ($k$ = 1 to 10) from $k$ raters of the panel drawn at random (each rater equally likely), with ratings generated from the fitted GRM and scored with its parameters, which were treated as known. The simulation used 50 replications of 2,000 simulated products per $k$ (seed 20260713). The table gives the empirical marginal reliability (mean and 95% range over replications) and the mean product-level reliability rel~post~. Because the parameters are treated as known, the ranges reflect simulation variability only, not parameter uncertainty.
